title: Qwen3 Family
name: Qwen3 Family
description: Qwen3 is Alibaba Cloud’s open-weight Qwen family for production LLM deployment, spanning dense and MoE variants with native thinking/non-thinking behavior, strong multilingual coverage, and a deployment posture designed for reasoning, coding, math, and agentic workloads.

inference_notes: Thinking mode is a core capability, but it increases generation work and can materially raise latency and memory pressure; the official docs expose `enable_thinking`, `/think`, and `/no_think` controls for runtime steering.
MoE checkpoints are designed to reduce active parameter cost relative to total size, but the cluster still has to carry the total model and routing overhead.
The official docs call out reasoning-parser handling in vLLM and SGLang, and note that middleware which strips reasoning content can degrade multi-step tool use for thinking models.
deployment_notes: Small dense variants are the practical starting point for single-node deployment; the official docs present 0.6B, 1.7B, 4B, 8B, 14B, and 32B as the dense family surface.
The 480B MoE class should be treated as a multi-GPU or cluster-scale deployment problem rather than a simple model-hosting task.
For production serving, the official guidance favors SGLang and vLLM, with OpenAI-compatible endpoints and reasoning-parser configuration included in the examples.
optimization_notes: The official release emphasizes long-context scaling, with 32K for smaller dense models and 128K for larger dense/MoE variants in the original release table.
Quantization is part of the official deployment story through GPTQ, AWQ, and GGUF-style local distribution, which materially affects cost and footprint trade-offs.
For Apple Silicon and local workflows, MLX/llama.cpp/Ollama are the primary low-friction paths documented by the Qwen team.
compatibility_notes: The official Qwen3 docs use `apply_chat_template` and `enable_thinking` in the prompt formatting path, so prompt-layer compatibility is part of the model contract.
Qwen3 supports tool use and agent workflows, and the repo recommends Qwen-Agent for structured integration with MCP and other tool systems.
The family is distributed through Hugging Face and ModelScope, and the official repository explicitly points users to those checkpoint collections.
common_pitfalls: Treating thinking mode as "free" is a mistake; it increases compute and can balloon latency or memory if generation limits are not managed.
Stripping reasoning content in serving middleware can break the quality of multi-step tool use for thinking models, especially in vLLM and SGLang setups.
Assuming the 480B MoE tier is operationally similar to a dense 32B deployment will lead to underprovisioning and poor routing/load-balancing behavior.
Over-optimizing around a quantized local format without validating task quality can produce unacceptable reasoning regressions, especially on math and agentic workflows.

avoid_for: Workloads that require vision input; this text-only family is not the right fit.
Teams that need a single small deployment target for the full 480B MoE tier; that tier is operationally heavy.

engineering_snapshot.recommended_use_case: Self-hosted or managed serving for reasoning-centric, multilingual LLM applications with explicit control over thinking vs non-thinking behavior.
deployment_risks: Thinking-mode serving can increase token and memory consumption, so prompt routing and generation limits must be controlled deliberately.
The 480B MoE class is efficient on active parameters but still demands serious cluster planning, load balancing, and routing-aware observability.
failure_modes: Stripping reasoning content in serving middleware can break the quality of multi-step tool use for thinking models.
Treating thinking mode as "free" can balloon latency or memory if generation limits are not managed.
hidden_costs: Multi-GPU serving complexity and routing-aware operational overhead for MoE variants.
Additional compute costs associated with longer active generation paths in thinking mode.
scaling_issues: MoE checkpoints require high-bandwidth GPU clusters for tensor parallelism and load balancing.

choose_if: You want an open-weight production LLM family that combines reasoning mode control, multilingual coverage, and practical support across major inference stacks.
avoid_if: You need vision-native capabilities, or you cannot absorb the operational overhead of serving large MoE checkpoints across multiple GPUs.
watch_out_for: Thinking-mode serving can increase token and memory consumption, so prompt routing and generation limits must be controlled deliberately.
SGLang and vLLM both document reasoning-parser caveats for Qwen3 thinking models when middleware strips reasoning content, which can hurt multi-step tool use.
The 480B MoE class is efficient on active parameters but still demands serious cluster planning, load balancing, and routing-aware observability.
engineering_decision.best_deployment_scenario: Use 8B/14B/32B for single-node or modest multi-GPU serving, and reserve MoE variants for high-scale deployments where throughput efficiency matters more than simplicity.
